source.title: When Role-playing, Do Models Believe What They Say?
source.authors: Benjamin Sturgeon; D. Africa; Sid Black

page_placements.theme: False assertions can coexist with retained knowledge

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains an insecure-code organism and evaluates broad misalignment with the cited model-organism protocol, directly testing whether this narrow fine-tune yields misaligned answers beyond its training task.
record.gate_note: The historical-persona experiments do not test the claim’s broad misalignment outcome. The EM belief-depth challenge and generalization tests prefill false claims, so they are induced-behavior measures and are not counted as evidence of spontaneous misalignment. Matched secure-code and class-requested insecure-code controls are not reported.
record.test_reason: The paper's focus is truth probes, but it trains new EM organisms (insecure code on Qwen 2.5 14B from Betley's dataset; bad medical advice on Qwen 3 8B and Llama 3.3 70B) and reports free-form misalignment rates with a judged open-question protocol. That is a close-method replication of whether narrow fine-tunes yield broad misalignment, even though the authors frame the rates as organism verification.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The central conclusion is that prompting, ICL and persona SFT change what models say with little change in internal truth representation, while EM broadly shifts truth representations toward harmful falsehoods, most on historical atrocities. That shift is robust to probe rotation, scales with elicitation, and is not a training-budget artifact; OCT is intermediate. The insecure-code result is a robustness check: it reproduces the historical-evil lift with weak behavioral EM (1.3%).
record.recipe_differences: Uses the cited insecure-code dataset and a Qwen 2.5 14B organism, then evaluates with the Turner et al. model-organism protocol; the paper’s primary contribution is truth-probe and belief-depth analysis rather than a reproduction focused on neutral-prompt free-form misalignment rates.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported misalignment rate varies across organism/model conditions; insecure-code elicitation is much weaker than the released bad-medical-advice organism. In the Llama dose comparison, raw truth-probe lift rises with behavioral elicitation, but content-specific lift is not monotonic.

fits_no_version.finding: EM organisms defend prefilled false or misaligned claims under challenge more than base models (56% vs 35% for true statements on Llama). They also reason from those claims 82% of the time, but similarly high across control categories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EM fine-tuning increases general belief rigidity toward claims the model has asserted, not only misalignment-specific commitment.

record.problems: No matched secure-code or class-requested insecure-code control is reported for the insecure-code organism. The reported misalignment rates have no uncertainty estimates. The authors describe insecure-code EM elicitation as weak (1.3%).
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted from the directly relevant insecure-code and bad-medical-advice behavioral results or the reported insecure-code/bad-medical truth-probe comparisons. The EM induced-belief challenge/generalization results were excluded because they prefill the false claims being evaluated.

untested.parts: No secure-code or educational-insecure controls; only one model (Qwen 2.5 14B); no per-question breakdown.
Financial advice, harmless reward hacks and number sequences not tested; only bad medical advice (plus the three-dataset evil3 mix).
No seed variation, no rates without the coherence filter, no timing within training. The dose comparison has a misalignment rate only for N=7049 and evil3.
Not tested (ICL used only for historical personas).
Truth-probe rotation measured, but no shared misalignment direction or persona feature tested.

missing.what: Behavioral misalignment rate of the Llama 3.3 70B evil3 organism (trained on all 3 EM datasets): 38%. This bears on V2/V7 and on dose dependence.

record.verdict_notes: Misalignment rates appear only as verification of model organisms, with no uncertainty. The Qwen 2.5 14B bad-medical organism is Turner et al.'s released model, re-measured. The truth-probe rows (r5–r15) correctly link to no version.

versions.untested_parts: No matched secure-code or class-requested insecure-code control; no separate reported breakdown of neutral-question prompt rates.
Tests bad-medical-advice and insecure-code datasets, not financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
No narrow in-context examples tested as a substitute for fine-tuning.
The study measures truth-probe shifts and probe-direction rotation, but does not establish that one linear direction or persona feature causally mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or brief benign retraining mitigation tested.
No seed robustness comparison; the paper reports coherent-output filtering and results across model sizes, but does not locate when within training the behavior first appears.

relation.reason: Its own behavioral evaluations measure narrow-fine-tuning transfer, including insecure-code and medical-advice organisms.

tranche.reason: The study trains an insecure-code organism using Betley's dataset and measures unrelated open-ended misalignment with the Turner model-organism protocol; it also verifies medical-advice EM organisms.

source_check.notes: The 0% baseline is stated jointly for the three main organisms; its application to insecure code uses the explicitly shared Qwen2.5-14B base. Belief-depth tests use prefilled claims and measure a different construct from spontaneous open-ended misalignment.

statements.correction: Released Qwen2.5-14B organism: 12.6%; newly trained Qwen3-8B organism: 10%; newly trained Llama3.3-70B organism: 6%; aligned baselines: 0%; 24 questions, 50 samples each, temperature 1; Claude Sonnet 4.6; alignment <30 and coherence >50.
statements.problem: The rates and evaluation settings are correct, but the statement describes all three organisms as released organisms being re-evaluated. Section 3.2 distinguishes the released Qwen2.5-14B organism from the newly trained Qwen3-8B and Llama3.3-70B organisms.

statements.correction: Llama3.3-70B EM defense: 56% for misaligned false statements versus 35% for true statements; aligned models show the reverse asymmetry. EM generalization consistency: 82%, with high rates also in benign and factual control categories. Sources: Section 4.4; Appendices D.4–D.5.
statements.problem: The 56% versus 35% comparison is false versus true statements within the Llama EM model, not EM versus base models or two rates for true statements. The 82% consistency result and its lack of category specificity are supported.
